planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; this naturally occurring witch's-broom sport was discovered on a standard sweetgum in Tennessee and stays remarkably narrow for its entire life.

directions: Slender Silhouette is an extremely narrow, columnar sweetgum selection that reaches 35 to 60 feet tall while spreading only 3 to 8 feet wide, making it one of the tightest fastigiate forms available among large deciduous shade trees. It carries the species' star-shaped foliage and turns the same mosaic of yellow, orange, red, and burgundy in fall, but its exclamation-point silhouette makes it useful as a living screen, an architectural accent, or a street tree in narrow planting strips where a normal sweetgum's broad canopy would not fit. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun and stake young trees loosely during establishment, since the narrow form can be more prone to wind lean before roots anchor. It still produces the species' spiny seed balls, so avoid siting directly over patios or walkways.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Plant of the Week

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Moraine is the most cold-hardy sweetgum selection available and extends reliable sweetgum fall color well north of the species' typical range.

directions: Moraine is a cold-hardy sweetgum selection, introduced from Moraine Farms in Ohio, prized for reliably surviving winters that damage seedling-grown sweetgum and for holding a neat, uniform narrow-pyramidal form when young that broadens with age. Its glossy, star-shaped leaves turn dependable shades of red, purple, yellow, and orange in fall, and it grows into a large shade tree well suited to parks, campuses, and spacious residential lots in the upper limits of the species' hardiness range. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; like other sweetgums it develops a taproot when young, so transplant container stock while small for the easiest establishment. It produces the species' spiny seed balls, so keep it away from walkways, patios, and mowed turf where the litter is a nuisance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese sweetgum tolerates more shade and a wider soil pH range than American sweetgum while offering a similar large-scale fall color display.

directions: Chinese sweetgum is an East Asian relative of American sweetgum, distinguished by its three-lobed (rather than five- to seven-lobed) leaves that emerge with a purplish flush in spring, mature to lustrous dark green through summer, and turn striking shades of red, orange, and purple in fall, often later in the season than the native species. It grows into a broad, rounded shade tree and tolerates partial shade, a wider range of soil pH, and warm, humid summers better than American sweetgum, making it a useful alternative large tree for parks, campuses, and spacious gardens across the warmer end of its hardiness range. Plant young container stock in moist, well-drained soil, since like other sweetgums it resents being moved once its taproot is established. It produces spiny seed balls similar to those of American sweetgum, so avoid planting directly over patios, walkways, or mowed turf.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, rich soil in full sun to mostly shade; Autumn Cascades is a semi-weeping female selection that develops a graceful cascading branch structure distinct from the upright habit of typical black gum.

directions: Autumn Cascades is a semi-weeping black gum selection whose pendulous, cascading branches give it strong sculptural presence year-round, in contrast to the pyramidal habit of typical seedling-grown black gum. As a female clone it produces the species' small blue-black fruit, valuable to songbirds, and displays the same early, reliable transition to yellow, orange, and scarlet fall foliage that makes black gum one of the best native fall-color trees. Plant in rich, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to considerable shade; black gum develops a deep taproot, so set out young container stock and avoid transplanting established trees. Its weeping habit and moderate mature size make it a good specimen for smaller landscapes where a full-sized upright black gum would be too large.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained to consistently damp soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese tupelo is smaller and more disease-resistant than American black gum while offering an even more vivid, earlier-arriving fall color display.

directions: Chinese tupelo is a smaller East Asian relative of American black gum, prized among tree collectors for new foliage that emerges bronze-purple before maturing to glossy green and then turning brilliant red, orange, and gold in fall, typically arriving earlier in the season than most native shade trees. It grows into a rounded to broadly pyramidal tree, generally more compact and more resistant to leaf spot diseases than Nyssa sylvatica, and it thrives in consistently moist to wet, acidic soils, making it well suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and other damp sites. Plant young container stock in spring, since like other tupelos it develops a deep taproot and dislikes being moved once established. Give it full sun to partial shade and avoid high-pH soils, which cause chlorosis in this genus.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Tupelo Tower Black Gum (Columnar Black Gum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tupelo Tower is the narrowest, most upright black gum selection available, useful where a full-spread black gum would not fit.

directions: Tupelo Tower is a narrow, strongly upright black gum selection from Klyn Nurseries in Ohio, chosen for its columnar branching structure and exceptional cold hardiness compared with other black gum cultivars. It carries the species' glossy summer foliage and turns dependable scarlet, orange, and yellow in fall, delivering the same outstanding autumn display as seedling black gum in a fraction of the width, which makes it useful for narrow side yards, street tree plantings, and screens where space is limited. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; black gum develops a deep taproot early, so transplant young container stock and avoid moving established trees. It needs minimal corrective pruning beyond removing occasional competing leaders to maintain its tight columnar form.

planting.note: Plant in full sun with ample overhead and root space in spring or fall; Columbia was bred by the USDA National Arboretum specifically for improved resistance to anthracnose and powdery mildew in demanding street-tree settings.

directions: Columbia is a London plane selection bred by the USDA National Arboretum specifically for strong resistance to sycamore anthracnose and powdery mildew, two diseases that regularly disfigure seedling-grown London planes and American sycamores in wet spring weather. It shares the species' vigorous growth, large maple-like leaves, and showy exfoliating camouflage-patterned bark, along with excellent tolerance of compacted urban soil, heat, drought, and pollution that makes London plane a mainstay street and park tree. Give it a large, uncontested root zone and full sun; established trees need little supplemental water beyond extended drought. Prune in the dormant season to remove crossing limbs and maintain clearance over streets and sidewalks, as with other large-canopy plane trees.
sources: USDA National Arboretum Floral and Nursery Plants Research Unit
North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in full sun with ample overhead and root space in spring or fall; Liberty is a USDA National Arboretum introduction selected alongside Columbia for improved anthracnose and powdery mildew resistance.

directions: Liberty is a U.S. National Arboretum Plant Introduction developed alongside Columbia to address the chronic anthracnose and powdery mildew problems of seedling-grown London plane, resulting in a vigorous, upright-pyramidal tree with good tolerance of heat, drought, and urban stress. Its large, five-lobed leaves and showy, camouflage-patterned exfoliating bark match the ornamental value of standard London plane, while its improved disease resistance keeps the canopy fuller and cleaner through wet spring weather that commonly defoliates susceptible trees. Give it a large uncontested root zone and full sun; established trees tolerate compacted soil, pollution, and road salt as well as other London plane selections. Prune in the dormant season to remove crossing limbs and maintain clearance in street-tree plantings.
sources: USDA National Arboretum Floral and Nursery Plants Research Unit

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental plane is one of the parent species of the London plane hybrid and becomes a massive, long-lived tree that requires ample space away from structures and pavement.

directions: Oriental plane is a long-lived, massive shade tree native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia, one of the two parent species of the widely planted London plane hybrid, sharing its deeply lobed, maple-like leaves and the same striking mottled bark that exfoliates in patches of cream, gray, and olive. It develops a broad, spreading, short-trunked canopy with age and is exceptionally long-lived, with venerable specimens in the Mediterranean region and Middle East documented at many centuries old. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun with generous overhead and root space, since it ultimately becomes too large for typical residential lots; it tolerates heat, drought once established, and a range of soil types better than many large shade trees. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood, as this species is best allowed to develop its naturally broad, picturesque form.
